    ENGIE AT A GLANCE




    ENGIE IS A WORLD LEADER
    IN THE ENERGY TRANSITION
    Accelerate the transition to a carbon-neutral economy

    Enshrined in the Group’s bylaws, “the purpose (raison d'être) of ENGIE is to act
    to accelerate the transition to a carbon-neutral economy, through low-energy solutions
    that are more respectful of the environment. This purpose brings together the company,
    its employees, customers and shareholders and reconciles economic performance
    and positive impact on people and the planet. ENGIE's action is assessed in its entirety
    and over time.”

     The material, speci c risks to which the Group is exposed, based on its own assessment, are described below. They are divided
     into seven categories:
     • political and regulatory risks;                                                          • operational risks;
     • risks deriving from climate and environmental issues;                                    • social and societal risks;
     • economic and competition risks;                                                          • risks relating to nuclear activities.

       3.1           SUSTAINABILITY STATEMENT

     ESRS ESSENTIALS




       ENGIE’S MATERIAL MATTERS
         ESRS E1     CLIMATE CHANGE                                                                         11 IROS(1)

       Climate change mitigation and energy transition                                                           1 negative impact    2 risks
       ENGIE is committed to achieving carbon neutrality by 2045. To that end, it is managing                    3 positive impacts   3 opportunities
       a sustained and steady reduction in its greenhouse gas emissions. The Group is investing
       signi cantly in developing renewable electricity and gas across its entire value chain,
       while simultaneously reducing its fossil fuel footprint.

       Adaptation to the consequences of climate change                                                                               2 risks
       Climate change leads to extreme weather events and, in the medium term, in uences the
       availability of natural resources (water, wind, sunlight, etc.) as well as customer needs (less
       heating, more cooling) that may impact ENGIE’s operating conditions and its business model.

         ESRS E2     INDUSTRIAL POLLUTION                                                                   7 IROS

       Air, soil and water pollution                                                                             3 negative impacts   3 risks
       ENGIE’s activities may generate emissions into the air, water and soil, which could impact                1 positive impact
       ecosystems and human health (e.g., energy production via combustion).

         ESRS E3     WATER                                                                                  5 IROS

       Preserving freshwater resources                                                                           2 negative impacts   2 risks
       ENGIE is dependent on freshwater resources to maintain its operations (e.g., CCGT,                                             1 opportunity
       hydroelectric dams). Controlling the pressures exerted on this resource is therefore key,
       particularly in water-stressed areas.

         ESRS E4     BIODIVERSITY AND ECOSYSTEMS                                                            6 IROS

       Ecosystem degradation and biodiversity loss                                                               3 negative impacts   2 risks
       The Group’s activities, particularly the construction and operation of energy                             1 positive impact
       infrastructure, can contribute to the disruption of terrestrial and aquatic biodiversity,
       and to the arti cialization of land.

         ESRS E5     RESOURCE USE AND CIRCULAR ECONOMY                                                      6 IROS

       Resource management: waste reduction and circular economy                                                 1 negative impact    2 risks
       ENGIE designs and operates large-scale energy assets that rely on sometimes critical                      1 positive impact    2 opportunities
       raw materials. The decommissioning of assets – particularly renewables – has therefore
       become strategic. In addition, innovating through circular solutions within industrial
       models, such as using waste heat or developing biomethane, enables the recycling of
       waste from production.



         ESRS S1     OWN WORKFORCE                                                                          15 IROS

      Activity                       Trend modeling
      Thermal generation             ENGIE has assessed the impact of climatic conditions on the performance (ef ciency and output)
      (gas‑ red power plants)        and availability of these plants (based on temperature and river ow thresholds to determine
                                     plant outages).

      Hydro generation               ENGIE uses hydro-climatic projections to assess production variations attributable to climate
                                     change. Projections by asset are based on simulated ow rates and technical characteristics
                                     for the asset.

      Solar generation               The impact of climate change is calculated by taking into account changes in solar irradiation
                                     and temperature, which affect module performance.

      Wind generation                The impact of climate change is calculated using power curves (depending on turbine type/model)
                                     that relate wind speed to available power.
                                     The effects of temperature are accounted for either by shutdown in the event of high
                                     temperatures or by a gradual decrease in production.

      Demand for heating             Demand for heating and cooling is calculated based on heating and cooling degree days,
      and cooling                    population density, and assumptions about commercial and residential buildings. Domestic
                                     hot water demand is also included.

      Targets related to climate change adaptation [E1-4]
      [E1-4 AR 31, 34a, b, c, d] To address its material impacts, risks and opportunities with regard to climate change, the Group has set
      the following targets:


      Targets related to the implementation of climate adaptation
      processes within ENGIE                                                2025 results          Target              Target time horizon

      Percentage of existing sites to have been subject to a physical       53%                   100%                2025
      risks assessment

      Percentage of existing sites subject to material climate risk         85%                   100%                2026
      with an adaptation plan

      Percentage of new projects with Executive Committee and Board         89%                   100%                2026
      of Directors validation threshold incorporating climate risk
      analysis prior to investment decision


      Measurement of target achievement began in 2025.
      The target for the percentage of existing sites to have been subject to a physical risks assessment was not achieved in 2025. This
      was mainly due to the fact that renewable sites below an arbitrary installed capacity threshold (20 MW) were excluded from the 2025
        scal year. This simpli cation was made in order to prioritize the largest sites, which are mechanically more exposed to climate risk.
      In 2026, new methods will be developed to enable a more detailed monitoring of the target.

      The carbon intensity of energy production (Scope 1) was 121kg CO2 eq./MWh eq. in 2025, compared with 107kg CO2 eq./MWh eq.
      in 2024.
      The Group's GHG emissions fell by 12 Mt CO2 eq. in 2025. This reduction is mainly due to lower emissions related to the volumes
      of gas and electricity sold by the Group (Scopes 3.3.A/3.3.D/3.11) and the impact of fossil fuel asset disposals (Scope 3.15).
      In January 2025, Engie sold 15.66% of its original 33% stake in SAFIEC, which operates the SAFI thermal power plant in Morocco.
      Engie has announced that it plans to exit the company's share capital by 2027, as part of its strategy to withdraw from coal. With
      a percentage holding of 17.67% as from the date of sale, SAFIEC has been removed from the Group's scope of consolidation, and
      its GHG emissions are therefore no longer included in the Group's carbon footprint. For information, emissions related to the SAFI
      thermal power plant, based on Engie's 2025 shareholding in the company, are estimated at 1 Mt CO2 eq.
      [AR46j] The Group also emitted 3.8 Mt of biogenic CO2 in 2025 (Scopes 1 and 3 combined), compared with 3.4 Mt of biogenic CO2
      in 2024.

      Dismantling sub-topic
      ENGIE is committed to responsible management of site dismantling. The dismantling of industrial assets chie y concerns the
      Renewables & Flex Power GBU (coal and gas- red power plants, wind and solar power) and Electrabel in the nuclear sector.
      Dismantling operations are managed locally.

[MDR-P]                         The ethics and compliance framework
Scope of application            The ethics and compliance framework applies to all Group entities. Group managers at all levels
[MDR-P 65b]                     ensure that these principles are properly applied (see Section 3.1.4.1.1). ENGIE’s Ethics Code of
                                Conduct is therefore applicable to all Group employees and managers and covers relations with
                                all Group third parties. The same is true for the ethics and compliance policies, procedures and
                                professional codes of conduct: all managers and employees are responsible, at their own level,
                                for the proper application of ENGIE’s ethics policies and principles, both within the Group and
                                in their relations with each of its third parties, irrespective of their type
                                These principles relating to the scope of application of ENGIE’s ethics and compliance system
                                are disclosed to all Group employees, managers and third parties in the Group’s Ethics Code
                                of Conduct (see Section 3.1.4.1.4)

implementation                  compliance policy and its implementation

3.2.1        Human rights vigilance approach
ENGIE’s Ethics, Compliance & Privacy Department, attached to the Group’s Legal and Ethics Department, itself under the oversight of
the Corporate Secretary, is directly responsible for the human rights component of the Vigilance Plan. It relies on the Legal and
Ethics functional line, and on other departments concerned by human rights issues, such as the Human Resources Department.

                                 • Reporting and subsequent analysis of HiPos (near-fatal incidents) related to electrical risks and of

b)   Speci c prevention and mitigation measures by priority environmental risk
Priority risks         Speci c measures
Climate change         ENGIE recognizes the threat posed by climate change as detailed in the 1.5°C report of the
mitigation             Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Controlling greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is
                       a major challenge for the Group. ENGIE has set emissions reduction targets in line with the Paris
                       Agreement. In May 2021, the Group committed to achieving the 2045 Net Zero Carbon objective for
                       all its direct and indirect emissions. All targets are available in Section 3.1.2.1.4 Targets related to
                       climate change mitigation.
                       The actions taken to achieve these objectives can be found in Section 3.1.2.1.4 List of actions for
                       implementing policies. The main actions are:
                       • exiting coal by 2027 at the latest, with the following order of merit: closure, conversion, then,
                         if this is not possible, sale, ensuring continuous stakeholder engagement as part of a just transition
                         approach (see Section 3.1.3.1 Respect for human rights - Just Transition Policy);
                       • reducing, greening or decarbonizing gas consumption and sales, while producing green and
                         decarbonized gas;
                       • greening or decarbonizing electricity and heat production, sales and consumption;
                       • transitioning energy networks (and in particular reducing methane emissions from gas networks).
                       The Group has also developed management tools, which are described in Section 3.1.2.1.3 Transition plan.
                       The main tools are:
                       • the de nition of limits on the main GHG emissions contributors from its activities (energy, gas and
                         electricity generation). They are set as milestones throughout the Group’s Net Zero Carbon pathway
                         (2030, 2035, 2040, 2045) and allocated to each GBU;
                       • the monitoring of these limits, which is ensured each year as part of the Medium Term Plan, through
                         which the GBU develop their decarbonization business strategy to stay within the limits set;
                       • the infra-annual monitoring of emissions that is carried out via a quarterly survey of the main
                         emissions contributors. It is integrated into the managerial dialogue on operational and nancial
                         performance as part of the Quarterly Business Reviews;
                       • in addition, any new investment decisions must be made in accordance with the limits allocated to
                         the GBU.

Industrial pollution   • Once the risks of water, air or soil pollution have been identi ed, they are addressed through mitigation
                         actions (avoid, reduce, compensate) integrated into environmental action plans.
                       • To minimize the risk of air, water and soil pollution, application of safety protocols and risk
                         management strategies, including preventive maintenance and the use of best available techniques.

                       Actions include:
                       • including air, water and soil pollution matters in project development;
                       • improving diagnosis/inventory of air, water and soil pollutants linked to industrial processes;
                       • remediation of former gas sites.

      Fresh water               Identi cation measures are as follows:
                                • Group sites using freshwater located in areas of high or extreme water stress are identi ed

                                Actions include:
                                • implementing water action plans to reduce impact on the resource, while considering the watershed
                                  context and local stakeholders. These actions are integrated into environmental action plans;
                                • identifying and carrying out actions to reduce freshwater consumption at existing sites;
                                • for each new project under examination, analyzing the water management risks and opportunities,

      and ecosystems            • for each Group activity, identifying material negative impacts related to land degradation,
                                  deserti cation or soil sealing, see Section 3.1.2.2.4 Biodiversity and ecosystems;
                                • establishing a list of material priority sites, categorized by identi ed impacts, dependencies
                                  and sensitive areas impacted. These sites are assessed based on ve levels of criticality, see
                                  Section 3.1.2.2.4 Biodiversity and ecosystems;
                                • carrying out dependency analyses regarding biodiversity and ecosystems across the value chain
                                  using the LEAP method and the Global Biodiversity Score.

                                Actions include:
                                • implementing action plans at material priority sites;
                                • applying the avoid-reduce-compensate sequence to development projects;
                                • implementing ecological management for all the Group’s industrial activities, in particular without
                                  the use of chemical phytosanitary products;
                                • implementing Nature-Based Solutions (NBS).

      Resource use              • Waste management is carried out in accordance with the order of eight actions de ned in the policy:
      and circular economy        eco-design, preservation, optimization, reuse, repair, recycling, innovation, empowerment. As with
                                  other environmental matters, risk mitigation actions are included in environmental action plans.

                                Actions include:
                                • continuing to implement the Material Risks Passport;
                                • promoting the circular economy and natural resources dimension in LCAs (resource optimization,
                                  waste reduction, carbon footprint reduction, value chain improvement, regulatory and societal
                                  expectations);
                                • developing energy recovery from industrial and tertiary processes, using local resources.

      3.2.4.1.3 Monitoring mechanisms, performance measurement and effectiveness reporting
      ESG due diligence processes and supplier risk assessments are consolidated and tracked via dedicated tools. This enables the monitoring
      of the total number of ESG analyses, their risk levels (high, medium or low), product coverage and year-on-year trends. All
      reviews are documented and updated as necessary. As part of this process, risk assessments are formally reviewed every three
      years as a general rule, with more frequent reviews for high-risk activities.

      c) Speci c prevention and mitigation measures for priority non-energy procurement risks

      Priority risks             Speci c measures
      Solar panel, battery       Several years ago, the Group introduced a speci c, in-depth vigilance action plan to identify and
      and wind turbine           manage these risks for certain purchases categories. The Group has agreed to ensure compliance
      procurement risk           with international laws and actively monitors the situation to ensure that no forced labor is used
                                 anywhere along its supply chain, particularly in China. In 2025, the Group continued to exercise
                                 enhanced vigilance (see also Section 2.2.5.1).
                                 The Group conducts rigorous ethical checks of its suppliers. To ensure supplier transparency, ENGIE
                                 has also established direct communication with each of them to assess their ability to commit and
                                 to share the most sensitive information. The main measures implemented include:
                                 • in-depth supplier due diligence by independent experts who pay particular attention to human
                                   rights matters;
                                 • supplier supply chain mapping and supporting documentation;
                                 • a written statement from suppliers not to use forced labor;
                                 • distribution of ethics surveys on forced labor, requiring suppliers to provide documentary
                                   evidence showing that they prohibit forced labor;
                                 • stronger contractual clauses (general audit clause, breach of contract in case of failure by suppliers
                                   to meet their obligations, supplier’s guarantee to comply with local and international regulations
                                   governing forced labor, from the procurement of commodities through to the delivery of a product);
                                 • participation in several industry initiatives (Solar Energy Industries Association in the United
                                   States, SolarPower Europe, WindEurope, Global Battery Alliance) in the solar, wind and battery
                                   sectors to share and improve risk management practices.

                            existing procurement processes by mandating enhanced measures to mitigate risks associated
                            with existing Group processes:
                            • The Manage Supplier Panel process:
                              • only quali ed suppliers can participate in the pre-selection process for ENGIE projects,
                              • supplier quali cation has been reinforced with regard to Health, Safety and Environment (HSE)
                                standards,
                              • monitoring of quali ed suppliers is managed via a dedicated dashboard accessible to buyers
                                and procurement leads.
                                ENGIE has deployed a rationalization strategy to concentrate its expenditure on a restricted
                                panel of suppliers in order to ensure long-term performance and compliance;
                            • the Source to Contract process:
                              • only quali ed suppliers are eligible to receive invitations to tender,
                              • supplier bid evaluation.
                              Bids are analyzed based on nancial, technical, health & safety and ESG criteria. Asset lifecycle
                              considerations are integrated into the evaluation.
                            • Each category of criteria is assigned a speci c weighting:
                              • Health-Safety: minimum 15%,
                                ESG: 5% to 10%, notably covering human rights, environmental risks, local content, carbon
                                footprint (CO₂), impact on nature and biodiversity, and, where applicable, stakeholder
                                management (local communities, trade unions).
                              • Health-Safety
                                Each bidder must provide a written declaration of commitment to all general and project-speci c
                                requirements. This declaration, signed by the supplier’s executive management, is also required
                                for prospective subcontractors.
                              • contractual clauses;

                            Each contract includes reinforced provisions:

                              • General right-to-audit clause,
                              • Termination in the event of a breach of supplier obligations,
                              • Guarantee of compliance with local and international regulations, as well as general and project-
                                speci c requirements.

      3.2.6       Whistleblowing and alert reporting system

      Stakeholder engagement and social dialogue
      ENGIE has established a whistleblowing mechanism in consultation with representative trade unions. The European Works
      Council and the Global Forum regularly review the Group-wide whistleblowing system and the summary of reports received (see
      Section 3.2.7.3 Stakeholder relations).


      How it works
      The Whistleblowing System is open to all employees, both permanent or temporary, and to all external stakeholders,
      since January 2019. An external service provider forwards the anonymous report to the Group for processing. Section 3.1.4.1.5
      Whistleblowing and reporting of ethics incidents provides further operational details.

3.2.7.2     Plan operational performance monitoring and measurement
Each entity must ensure that the Vigilance Plan has been effectively rolled out within its scope. Internal control cycles and the
annual Ethics Compliance Report integrate the monitoring of these actions at the entity level (see Section 3.1.4.1.7 Controls and
certi cations). Since 2020, a dedicated internal control checkpoint for the deployment of the Vigilance Plan has been in place.
Speci c internal control checkpoints for individual actions (human rights, health & safety, ESG and procurement) provide further
monitoring of the deployment of Vigilance Plan initiatives.

      4.1           GOVERNANCE ORGANIZATION AND OPERATIONS
         SEPARATION OF THE ROLE OF CHAIRMAN AND CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER
         In 2016, ENGIE's Board of Directors opted to separate the functions of Chairman of the Board of Directors and Chief Executive
         Of cer in order to ensure a balance of powers in line with best corporate governance practices and to strengthen the
         effectiveness of the Group's governance. This choice, proven over time, is designed to ensure solid, collective governance that
         is fully adapted to ENGIE's strategic challenges.

      4.1.2.2     Duties of the Board of Directors
      The Board of Directors, on a collective basis, determines the Company's business strategy and oversees its implementation.
      Subject to the applicable laws and regulations and the Company bylaws, it determines the supervisory framework of Executive
      Management. It exercises the following powers [ESRS 2 - GOV-1]:


      Governance          • choosing the Executive Management system.
      Appointments        • appointing the executive corporate of cers and setting their compensation;
      and Compensation    • reviewing, at least once a year, the professional and salary equality policy.
      Strategy            • ensuring that shareholders and investors receive relevant, balanced and instructive information about
                            the Company's strategy and development model, the handling of signi cant non- nancial issues
                            and the Company's long-term prospects;
                          • reviewing, at least once a year, the Group's industrial strategy and nancial strategy.
      Finance             • dealing with all matters concerning the ef cient running of the Company and, through its decisions,
                            managing the Company's business;
                          • performing any checks and veri cations it considers appropriate;
                          • reviewing, at least once a year, the budget.
      ESG                 • working to promote long-term value creation by the company by taking into consideration the social
                            and environmental challenges of its activities as well as its purpose;
                          • reviewing, at least once a year, market trends, the competitive context and principal challenges, including
                            in the area of the Group's social and environmental responsibility.

  STRATEGIC PLANNING SEMINAR
  The Board held its annual strategic planning seminar in June 2025. The seminar included a presentation of the Group's
  downstream strategy and an overview of the Supply & Energy Management (S&EM) GBU, followed by a discussion of S&EM's
  growth drivers, with a focus on BtoB dynamics and BtoC transformation. A segment was also devoted to digital strategy
  and arti cial intelligence (AI) to enhance ENGIE's operational performance, and to the Group's data center strategy.

  EXECUTIVE SESSIONS
  Closed meetings of Directors with no executive functions take place regularly before Board meetings. These meetings, known
  as Executive Sessions, cover a range of topics. The Audit Committee and the ACGC are systematically preceded, or followed,
  by a meeting reserved for their members, without management present.

The Audit Committee has       ve members: Ross McInnes(1) (Chairman), Christophe Agogué, Céline Fornaro Michel Giannuzzi(1),
Marie‑José Nadeau(1).
The Audit Committee met six times in 2025, with an attendance rate of 100%.
The Executive Vice-President in charge of Finance, ESG and Procurement and the Vice-President in charge of Group Audit
attended all the meetings of the Audit Committee. The Statutory Auditors attended all the meetings. Pursuant to Article 5.1.1 of
the Internal Rules of the Board of Directors, the Chair of the EESDC is invited to every meeting of the Audit Committee that
addresses reporting on non- nancial information.
Each meeting of the Committee was followed by an executive session.
The Committee reports regularly to the Board of Directors on the performance of its tasks. It also reports on the results of the
audit assignment, how it contributed to the completeness of the nancial information and the role it played in this process. The
Committee also monitors the process of preparing non- nancial information. It immediately noti es the Board of Directors of any
problems encountered.
The period between the examination of the accounts by the Audit Committee and the closing of the accounts by the Board of
Directors is at least 48 hours.
In accordance with the provisions of the Afep-Medef Code, and taking into account their professional and academic backgrounds,
the members of the Audit Committee have the necessary knowledge and expertise to be considered as having the nancial and/
or accounting skills as de ned by Article L.821-67 of the French Commercial Code (Code de commerce). Their combined
experience gives them an informed understanding of the nancial issues, accounting mechanisms, and internal control and audit
frameworks that fall within the Committee’s remit.

       NOTE 3 INVESTMENTS IN EQUITY METHOD ENTITIES
        ACCOUNTING STANDARDS
        The Group accounts for its investments in associates and joint ventures using the equity method. Under IFRS 11 – Joint
        Arrangements, a joint venture is a joint arrangement whereby the parties that have joint control of the arrangement have
        rights to the net assets of the arrangement. An associate is an entity over which the Group has signi cant in uence.

      16.4      Capital management
      ENGIE SA seeks to optimize its nancial structure at all times      The Group's policy is to maintain a “strong investment grade”
      by pursuing an optimal balance between its economic net            rating from the rating agencies. To achieve this, it manages its
      debt and its EBITDA. The Group's key objective in managing           nancial structure in line with the indicators usually
      its nancial structure is to maximize value for shareholders        monitored by these agencies, namely the Group's operating
      and reduce the cost of capital, while ensuring that the Group      pro le, nancial policy and a series of nancial ratios. One of
      has the nancial exibility required to continue its expansion.      the most commonly used ratios is the ratio where the
      The Group manages its nancial structure and makes any              numerator includes operating cash ows less cost of debt and
      necessary adjustments in light of prevailing economic              taxes paid, and the denominator includes adjusted net
      conditions. In this context, it may choose to adjust the             nancial debt. Net nancial debt is mainly adjusted for
      amount of dividends paid to shareholders, reimburse a              nuclear provisions and provisions for pensions, as well as for
      portion of capital, carry out share buybacks (see Note 16.1.2      50% of hybrid debt (deeply-subordinated perpetual notes).
      Treasury stock), issue new shares, launch share-based              In addition, the Group has issued a guidance targeting an
      payment plans, recalibrate its investment budget, or sell          “economic net debt to EBITDA” ratio less than or equal to 4x.
      assets in order to scale back its nancial net debt.
                                                                         The Group’s objectives and processes for managing capital

                                                                         capital requirements except those provided for by law.

6         Financial Information
          Statutory auditors’ report on the consolidated   nancial statements




        • through 2050, the retention of its gas infrastructure
          network or its conversion to enable the supply of green
          gases (biomethane, hydrogen, etc.) that will gradually
          replace natural gas
        • the Multi-Year Energy Schedule (PPE3), Programmation
          Pluriannuelle de l’Energie (PPE3) adopted by decree on
          February 13, 2026, which introduces measures to reduce
          gas consumption and, in particular, a major objective to
          replace gas boilers with alternative energy solutions and
          particularly electricity. Your Group considers this
          objective to be unrealistic due to its economic sustainability
          for households and because of technical constraints that
          do not allow the installation of ef cient electrical
          solutions or the connection to a heating network in almost
          half of dwellings. Therefore, your Group considers that
          the PPE3 does not call into question the energy mix
          scenario for 2050;
        • cash ow projections established using tariffs negotiated
          with the regulator (CRE) and terminal values corresponding
          to the expected value of the regulated asset base (RAB)
          for the valuation of its activities in France.
      • goodwill of the Nuclear operating segment, in the context of
        the implementation of the so-called Phoenix law, for which
        your Group has taken the following into account:
        • the ten-year extension beyond 2025 of the operation of
          the Doel 4 and Tihange 3 units only within a dedicated
          legal structure, equally owned by the Belgian State and
          your Group, according to an economic model based on a
          contract for difference mechanism;
        • an assumed ten-year extension, of drawing rights for
          nuclear power plants in France.

      • the US assets of the Renewables & Batteries and Local
        Energy Infrastructures RoW operating segments in light of
        regulatory changes introduced by the One Big Beautiful Bill
        Act, which provides for the planned phase-out of renewable
        energy subsidies. Your Group has analyzed the viability of
        projects currently under development.

      Other operating receivables
      Other operating receivables include the current account with ENGIE Finance, as well as margin calls. Items for which there is a
      risk of non-collection are written down.


      Marketable securities
      Marketable securities are shown on the balance sheet at cost.
      When the market value of securities at December 31 is lower than their book value, a write-down is recognized for the difference.
      For listed securities, market value is determined based on the market price at the end of the reporting period.

      6.1       Natural gas reserves
      Gas reserves at end-December 2025 were €347 million lower than at end-December 2024, mainly due to a fall in both average
      prices and inventory quantities between December 2024 and December 2025.
